reason: Przybylski's Star is supported across multiple independent sources by dozens of verified, cross-cited facts detailing its discovery, extreme spectrum, and ongoing scientific controversy.
story: In 1961, astronomer Antoni Przybylski pointed a telescope at a faint star 356 light-years away in Centaurus and found a spectrum that broke every rule of stellar astrophysics. Instead of showing normal amounts of iron and nickel, HD 101065 was packed with rare-earth elements like holmium at thousands of times solar abundances. Even stranger, researchers later reported absorption lines belonging to short-lived radioactive elements—including plutonium, americium, and promethium, an element whose longest-lived isotope decays in just under eighteen years. Because stars live for billions of years, these elements should have vanished eons ago, sparking theories ranging from undiscovered superheavy elements on a nuclear 'island of stability' to extraterrestrial civilizations dumping radioactive waste into their sun. While 2023 reanalyses suggest extreme line blending may explain away some radioactive claims, Przybylski's Star remains an extraordinary, slow-turning cosmic puzzle.
angle: A star 356 light-years away appears to shine with short-lived radioactive elements like plutonium and promethium that decay in mere decades and shouldn't exist in a billion-year-old star.

claims.claim: Przybylski's Star is designated in astronomical catalogues as HD 101065.
The star is located in the southern constellation Centaurus.
The star sits approximately 356 light-years away from Earth.
The star was first catalogued in 1873 by astronomer Benjamin Apthorp Gould.
Polish-Australian astronomer Antoni Przybylski discovered the star's peculiar spectrum in 1961.
Przybylski first reported the star's unusual spectrum in a 1961 paper in Nature.
The star's spectral features would not fit into the standard stellar classification framework.
The star's atmosphere displays an extreme overabundance of rare-earth lanthanide elements.
Rare-earth elements in the star are enriched by roughly 1,000 times or more compared to solar levels.
Common iron-group elements like iron and nickel are unusually weak or depleted in the star's spectrum.
The star shows prominent absorption lines of the rare-earth element holmium.
Donald Kurtz discovered in 1978 that the star exhibits rapid photometric pulsations.
Przybylski's Star is the prototype and first recognized member of the rapidly oscillating Ap (roAp) variable star class.
The star pulsates photometrically on a rapid cycle of roughly 12 minutes.
The star possesses an intense magnetic field measuring over 2 kilogauss.
Modeling of the star's magnetic field indicates an extraordinarily slow rotation period tentatively estimated at about 188 years.
Spectroscopic studies reported absorption lines attributed to short-lived actinides, including plutonium and americium.
Promethium, an unstable element with no stable isotopes and a longest half-life of roughly 17.7 to 18 years, was reported in the star's spectrum.
Technetium, an unstable radioactive element, was also reported in the star's spectrum.
Reanalyses, including a 2023 study, failed to confirm the presence of promethium or technetium due to heavy spectral line blending.
Physicists proposed that radioactive decay from a hypothetical 'island of stability' of superheavy elements could account for short-lived actinides.
The star has been discussed in SETI research as a candidate for artificial salting or nuclear waste dumping by an extraterrestrial civilization.
The star has an estimated mass of about 1.5 solar masses.
The star is estimated to be around 1 to 2 billion years old and near the end of its main-sequence lifetime.

disputed: Detections of short-lived radioactive elements (promethium, technetium, and transuranic actinides): Reported in several spectroscopic studies, but recent reanalyses (such as Andrievsky et al. 2023) found no confirmed lines because severe rare-earth line crowding mimics these signals. A script should clearly state that detections of elements like promethium remain unconfirmed and heavily contested.

Rotation period of 188 years: While calculated from decades of longitudinal magnetic field measurements, astronomers explicitly describe this period as tentative and not a unique mathematical solution. A script should qualify it as 'a tentative estimate derived from magnetic data.'

Alien nuclear waste dumping / SETI marker: Speculative concept originating in 1960s-1980s SETI literature (Sagan, Shklovskii, Whitmire). There is no empirical evidence of artificial intervention; astronomers favor natural mechanisms like atomic diffusion or nuclear spallation. A script should treat extraterrestrial claims strictly as thought-experiment speculation.

Potential binary companion: An optical companion was detected 8 arcseconds away, but Gaia astrometry confirmed it is an unrelated background star more than twice as far away. A script should avoid claiming Przybylski's Star is a physical binary.
